extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, discourse analysts, journalism researchers and students
extracted.subtask_description: A multimodal discourse-analytic framework for identifying and coding the ways newsworthiness is constructed in language and images; used to analyse how events are 'sold' as news via linguistic and visual markers. Suitable for qualitative and systematic analysis of news texts and photographs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negativity
rubrics_metrics.description: Negative aspects of an event (death, damage, conflict, scandal, crisis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructed through evaluative language (e.g. 'disaster,' 'tragedy'), images of destruction, and other lexical/semiotic signals of harm or loss. Use of negative evaluative adjectives, verbs, and visual depictions that foreground loss or danger are markers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness
rubrics_metrics.description: Relevance to the present (immediacy, currency, seasonality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marked by temporal expressions such as 'today,' 'now,' 'yesterday,' use of recent-tense verbs, references to anniversaries or current seasons/events. Look for lexical and grammatical cues that locate the event as current or immediate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proximity
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marked by place names, references to 'here,' localising language, cultural touchstones, and national references. Proximity can be signalled via emphasis on local actors, locales, or cultural relevance to the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superlativeness
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marked by intensifiers ('massive,' 'unprecedented'), quantifications, comparatives and superlatives. Language that amplifies scale, extremity or uniqueness is a cue to superlativeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliteness
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marked by titles, role labels (CEO, president), credentialing and references to institutional position. The presence of elite actors or authoritative sources signals newsworthiness via status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Effects or consequences of an event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marked by causal language, references to consequences, statistics indicating affected numbers, or explicit predictions of effects. Look for language that foregrounds who or what is affected and how.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marked by words like 'first,' 'unprecedented,' 'shocking,' 'surprise' and by presenting events as atypical or breaking precedent. Emphasis on rarity or deviation from expectation is the key signal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Human face or personal angles on a story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marked by inclusion of named individuals, quoted ordinary people, emotional details, anecdotes and human-interest framing. Personal names, biographical detail and emotive language are typical markers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consonance
rubrics_metrics.description: Stereotypicality; fitting expectations or familiar narratives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marked by stock phrases, references to recurring story types, and narrative patterns that align with audience expectations. Stories that fit pre-existing frames or tropes are consonant and therefore newsworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic Appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual attractiveness and dramatic quality (applied to images/photographs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For photographs: composition, color, framing, lighting and dramatic visual qualities are evaluated. Added in the authors' photograph analysis as a multimodal news value; look at visual design choices that make an image striking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytical perspectives: Cognitive vs Discursive
rubrics_metrics.description: Two complementary perspectives for understanding news values: Cognitive (news values as criteria journalists apply) and Discursive (news values as properties constructed in/through texts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The cognitive view treats values as selection criteria used by journalists; the discursive view (the basis of DNVA) examines how values are constructed through linguistic and multimodal resources in the news text. DNVA operationalises the discursive perspective by identifying textual and visual markers of each news value, though researchers may reference both perspectives in analysis.
